title: Switching costs
hook: switching between tasks costs time and accuracy, even when it seems fast

segments.voice: Yesterday, the phone on the table, and a line to carry: another room. Did the phone spend any part of the day out of sight? Was anything different while it was gone? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-two.

Three tabs open. An email half written. A text that just buzzed. A spreadsheet waiting underneath it all. A quick glance here, a reply there, back to the email, over to the sheet. To the person doing it, this can seem nimble, even fast. Psychologists who study attention have a dry name for what all that hopping charges you: switching costs. In their experiments, people asked to swap back and forth between two simple jobs get slower and make more mistakes than people who stay with one. And the odd part is how quiet the charge is. The switch seems instant. The bill arrives later, in small coins. Today is about that bill.
screen: `THREE TABS AND A BUZZING TEXT.` → `IT SEEMS FAST.` → `THE BILL ARRIVES IN SMALL COINS.`

segments.voice: Start with the lab. In a common kind of task-switching study, people see a number or a letter and make a quick judgment about it. Sometimes the rule stays the same from one trial to the next. Sometimes it changes. On the trials where the rule changes, answers come more slowly and with more errors. Researchers call that gap the switch cost. Next, why it happens. One explanation researchers give is that the mind has to put down one set of rules and pick up another, a kind of reloading. Warning people that a switch is coming makes the cost smaller. In some studies, though, a piece of it stays even when people know exactly what's next. Now step out of the lab and into an old letter. The Roman philosopher Seneca, writing to his friend Lucilius about reading too many books and traveling too much, puts it in three words: "Everywhere means nowhere." He wasn't measuring reaction times. He was describing a mind that never settles long enough to arrive. Finally, an honest limit. Lab tasks are tiny, and a real workday is not a lab. How much these small costs add up across an ordinary afternoon is still argued over, and researchers disagree about the size. The modest takeaway is this: each switch has some price, and some switches are worth paying for. The ones that aren't are often the small, automatic ones, the glance at a message that could have waited an hour. Fewer switches, chosen on purpose. That's the whole idea.
screen: `A SWITCH IS NOT FREE.` · `THE MIND RELOADS THE RULES.` · then, large: `EVERYWHERE MEANS NOWHERE.` · then: `FEWER SWITCHES, CHOSEN ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one thing at a time. Before the bell, pick two moments later today when you'll check and answer your messages together, a batch, instead of one by one as they arrive. Say the two times to yourself once. Then let the sit be a single task. Your only job is the breath. When attention jumps to a message, a plan, a noise, simply notice that it switched, and come back to the breath, one more time. No scorekeeping. Just one task, again and again. The bell holds the time.
Switching costs. The time and accuracy lost when the mind changes from one task to another, even when the change seems quick. Today's word.
Your line: one at a time. Today, answer your messages in two or three batches, at the times you picked, instead of the moment each one lands. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: People who take task-switching research to heart often batch their email and messages into set times of day, and some contemplative teachers frame doing one thing at a time as a practice in its own right.

original.note: Seneca's Latin, Letter 2: the one who is everywhere is nowhere.

trapdoor: what you thought: doing several things at once is just efficient.

notes: Confirm Gummere's wording for Letter 2.2: 'Everywhere means nowhere.' and the Latin 'Nusquam est qui ubique est.'
Seneca's context (reading too many authors, constant travel) is paraphrased; confirm.
Claim that warning/preparation shrinks the switch cost but leaves a 'residual' cost reflects Rogers & Monsell's findings; confirm the plain wording.
'Researchers disagree about the size' of real-world costs is a general characterization; a reviewer may want a source or a softer phrase.
The outline's 'feels fast' was reworded to 'seems fast' to avoid telling the listener what they feel.
